title: Breast Lump - Assessment and Triple Test
patient_instructions: You are Jane Thompson, a 40-year-old office administrator. You noticed a lump in your left breast about two weeks ago while showering, and you are frightened it might be cancer because a friend was recently diagnosed. You found it suddenly and have not had a breast lump before. It is not painful, and you have not noticed any nipple discharge, skin dimpling, redness, or change in shape. You have had no fever, no weight loss, and no loss of appetite. You have no lumps in your armpits or neck that you have felt. Your periods are regular; the lump does not obviously change with your cycle. You have never been pregnant and are not breastfeeding. No family history of breast or ovarian cancer. You are a non-smoker, drink one glass of wine a week, and take no regular medications or hormones. You have never had breast surgery or chest radiation. IDEAS: you fear cancer. CONCERNS: 'Am I going to die?' and 'Will I lose my breast?' EXPECTATIONS: you want to know what it is and what happens next. Affect: anxious, tearful if cancer is mentioned bluntly; reassured by a calm, structured explanation. If the candidate proposes tests, ask 'Do I really need a biopsy if the scan looks benign?'
candidate_instructions: You are a GP in a community practice. Jane Thompson, 40, presents worried about a breast lump she found two weeks ago. Her physical examination findings are provided on the screen: a 1.5 cm hard, lobulated, non-tender, immobile lump in the left upper outer quadrant, no lymphadenopathy. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, explain your provisional diagnosis and differentials to the patient, and outline your initial management plan including the triple test and referral pathway. Use language the patient can understand.
examiner_instructions: Assess whether the candidate takes a structured breast-lump history (timing, characteristics, nipple/skin change, systemic red flags, family history of breast AND ovarian cancer, hormonal/reproductive history, risk factors). The candidate should identify breast cancer as the primary concern given the hard, lobulated, immobile, non-tender mass, and give a sensible differential (fibroadenoma, fibrocystic change, fat necrosis, cyst). Expect a clear explanation of the triple test as three components (clinical assessment, imaging, non-excisional biopsy) whose CONCORDANCE matters - do not reward candidates who insist on a rigid 1-2-3 sequence. Candidate must arrange imaging appropriate to age (ultrasound plus mammography around age 40) AND biopsy even if imaging looks benign, and refer to a breast surgeon for this suspicious lump. Prompt only if stuck: 'What would you tell her about the next steps?'

criteria: Explores lump characteristics (onset, single/multiple, size, consistency, mobility, pain, skin/nipple change)
Screens breast-cancer red flags (nipple discharge and colour, skin dimpling/peau d'orange, axillary/neck nodes, weight/appetite loss)
Takes family history of both breast and ovarian cancer and hormonal/reproductive risk factors
Uses empathic, structured opening and gains rapport with an anxious patient
Identifies breast cancer as the leading concern given hard, lobulated, immobile, non-tender mass
Gives an appropriate differential (fibroadenoma, fibrocystic change, fat necrosis, cyst, lipoma)
Explains that triple-test concordance - not a fixed sequence - establishes the diagnosis
Arranges age-appropriate imaging (ultrasound plus mammography at age 40) AND core biopsy/FNA even if imaging appears benign
Refers to a breast surgeon for this clinically suspicious lump
Provides safety-netting (persistent lump, bloodstained/incomplete cyst aspirate, spontaneous single-duct bloody discharge, non-resolving 'mastitis') mandates urgent review
Explains diagnosis and plan in lay terms, checks understanding, and manages the patient's fear sensitively

red_flags: Hard, irregular/lobulated, fixed, non-tender lump - features highly suspicious of malignancy requiring biopsy regardless of imaging
Spontaneous unilateral bloodstained or serous single-duct nipple discharge (especially age 60+)
Skin dimpling/peau d'orange, nipple retraction, or axillary/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
Incompletely aspirated or bloodstained cyst, or a lump persisting after aspiration
A presumed lactational mastitis/abscess that does not resolve after appropriate antibiotics - inflammatory breast cancer must be excluded by imaging and biopsy
australian_guidelines: Cancer Australia / NBCF 'Investigation of a new breast symptom' pathway: assess every discrete breast lump with the triple test (clinical assessment, imaging, non-excisional biopsy); concordance of all three components guides management

Australian imaging practice: ultrasound is first-line in women under ~35 (dense tissue); mammography +/- ultrasound from ~35 upward, with both modalities commonly used around age 40; a suspicious lump is imaged and biopsied regardless of age

John Murtagh General Practice (8th ed): immediate referral to a breast surgeon for any positive triple-test component, incomplete cyst aspiration, or spontaneous unilateral single-duct bloody/serous discharge

Strong family history (early-onset or multiple first-degree relatives with breast/ovarian cancer, known BRCA1/BRCA2) warrants referral to a family cancer/genetics service and may alter screening (earlier age, MRI)
learning_objectives: Take a structured focused history for a breast lump including malignancy red flags and family cancer risk
Apply the Australian triple test correctly, understanding that component concordance rather than a fixed sequence determines diagnosis
Recognise that a clinically suspicious lump or a solid lesion on imaging still requires biopsy
Identify referral criteria to a breast surgeon and appropriate safety-netting
key_points: A 'benign-looking' fibroadenoma on examination and ultrasound still warrants completion of the triple test with biopsy
In a breastfeeding woman with a persistent lump, still consider inflammatory breast cancer and add galactocele to the differential
CA of the breast can present without pain - absence of pain is not reassuring
Correlate cytology/histology with clinical and imaging findings before reassuring or discharging

citations.claim: Even a young woman with a clinically and sonographically benign-looking lump warrants completion of the triple test/biopsy, and management must correlate cytology/histology with clinical and imaging findings.
citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment.pdf, p.294

citations.claim: Immediate referral to a breast surgeon is essential for any positive component of the triple test, incomplete cyst aspiration, or spontaneous unilateral bloody/serous single-duct discharge.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2523

citations.claim: Ultrasound is superior to mammography in young women, FNAC distinguishes benign versus malignant and cystic versus solid, and the breasts must always be examined even when the history suggests a benign cause.
citations.source: Churchills Pocketbook of Differential Diagnosis, p.56

citations.claim: Nipple discharge and other tell-tale breast cancer symptoms require a structured diagnostic strategy (discharge colour, nipple/skin change, asymmetry).
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2507
